c.tagline: Ancient temples and buzzing motorbike-filled boulevards.

emergency.note: Fire is 114; English-speaking operators are rare, so ask hotel staff to call or use a private clinic's hotline.

hood_landmark.Hoan Kiem (Old Quarter): Hoan Kiem Lake with Ngoc Son Temple on its islet
hood_landmark.Ba Dinh: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum on Ba Dinh Square
hood_landmark.Tay Ho (West Lake): Tran Quoc Pagoda on the shore of West Lake
hood_landmark.Dong Da: The Temple of Literature, Vietnam's first university
hood_landmark.Cau Giay: The Vietnam Museum of Ethnology's tribal-house exhibits

avoid.reason: Taxi/cyclo overcharging and shoeshine/fruit-seller scams in the Old Quarter; bag-snatching — use Grab

hood_desc: Hoan Kiem (Old Quarter) is the dense, atmospheric historic heart wrapped around the lake, packed with street food, night markets and colonial buildings; ideal for first-time visitors who want to walk everywhere and be in the middle of the action.

Ba Dinh is the stately political and administrative district home to the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum, embassies and grand boulevards; calmer and greener than the Old Quarter, it suits travelers who want history and quiet within reach of the center.

Tay Ho (West Lake) is the leafy, laid-back expat enclave along Hanoi's largest lake, full of cafes, boutiques, lakeside restaurants and international eateries; best for longer stays, families and those wanting a relaxed, upscale base away from the crush.

Dong Da is a large, densely local residential district with universities, markets and the Temple of Literature nearby; authentic and affordable with few tourists, it suits budget travelers and those wanting everyday Hanoi life.

Cau Giay is a modern western district of high-rises, malls, tech offices and student housing; practical, less scenic and well-priced, it fits business travelers and long-term visitors who prioritize new amenities over old-town charm.

water.note: Avoid tap water; use bottled or boiled water, even for brushing teeth.

transit.pay: Buy a paper ticket or reloadable smart card at station counters/machines, or use the MeGO virtual card in supported banking apps to tap in with a phone. Single rides cost about 8,000-15,000 VND depending on distance (~$0.30-0.60); a day pass is about 40,000 VND (~$1.60).
transit.hours: Trains run daily about 5:30am-10pm; there is no night service.

Public Bus 07 to Cau Giay, approx 1 hr

landmarks: Hoan Kiem Lake & Turtle Tower
The scenic heart of Hanoi's Old Quarter, its misty lake and small turtle-tower islet are among the most photographed views in the city.
The Huc Bridge & Ngoc Son Temple
A vivid red wooden bridge leading to a lakeside temple, offering one of Hanoi's most iconic color-pop photo compositions.
Temple of Literature (Van Mieu)
Vietnam's first national university, with tranquil courtyards, stone stelae on turtles, and classic Confucian architecture.
Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum
A monumental granite structure on Ba Dinh Square, iconic for its solemn Soviet-inspired architecture and ceremonial guard.
One Pillar Pagoda
A tiny wooden pagoda balanced on a single stone pillar rising from a lotus pond, a uniquely graphic architectural landmark.
Hanoi Opera House
A grand French colonial-era building with a striking neoclassical facade, especially photogenic at dusk when lit up.
St. Joseph's Cathedral
A twin-spired neo-Gothic cathedral built in the 1880s, its weathered stone facade a striking contrast to the surrounding Old Quarter streets.
Hanoi Old Quarter (36 Streets)
A maze of narrow streets packed with colorful shophouses, tangled wires, and street life, capturing the city's chaotic charm.
Long Bien Bridge
A historic cantilever bridge over the Red River, its rust-red steel trusses framing dramatic sunrise and sunset shots.
Hanoi Train Street
A narrow residential lane where trains squeeze between houses just inches away, a surreal and widely photographed scene.

train.note: The one international train, an overnight sleeper to Nanning in China with onward China Railway connections, leaves from Hanoi's Gia Lâm station - you need a paper Chinese visa in advance, as e-visas are not accepted at this border. The through Hanoi to Beijing service has not resumed. Domestically, Hanoi is the hub for sleeper trains to Sapa (Lào Cai), Huế and Đà Nẵng, and the Reunification Express to Ho Chi Minh City. Book on dsvn.vn, which takes foreign cards, or at Hanoi station on Le Duan.

intl.to: Vientiane & Savannakhet (Laos) - from Nước Ngầm and Mỹ Đình stations
intl.op: Vietnamese and Lao cross-border operators, tickets via VeXeRe

bus.note: Cross-border sleeper coaches to Vientiane (about 24 hours) and Savannakhet in Laos leave from Hanoi's Nước Ngầm and Mỹ Đình bus stations; many companies sell this route and rattletrap scam buses are common, so buy at the station or through a reputable agent rather than a street tout. There is no single official English booking site - VeXeRe is the standard Vietnamese platform and the most reliable way to compare departures. For China, Apec Travel runs several daily buses between Nanning and its office at 55 Trần Khát Chân St on the south side of the centre, around 8 hours including a change of bus and border formalities, though the overnight train is more comfortable.

ferry.note: Hanoi is an inland river city with no ferries or international boats. Halong Bay and Lan Ha Bay overnight cruises, about 3 hours east by road, are tourist trips rather than transport; for Cát Bà island, travel to Hải Phòng and take a local ferry or speedboat from there.
